summary: A cron-job monitor you run yourself: every scheduled job gets a URL it pings when it finishes, the monitor flips a job to late and then down when the pings stop, one chat message goes out per state change, and a dashboard shows every job with its last ping and a 24-hour histogram. When every item is ticked you have Healthchecks-style monitoring for a few dollars of hosting.

stack.why: no framework and no ORM: a ping is one INSERT and the loop is a setInterval
one file, survives restarts, fast enough for millions of pings
the channel you already watch, no SMS provider bill

stack.choice: A VPS that is not the box running your jobs
stack.why: a monitor on the same host reports nothing when that host dies

prerequisites.name: Node.js 22 or newer
prerequisites.why: Everything in this build runs on it: the server, the scripts, the tests.
prerequisites.get: Download the LTS installer from nodejs.org, or install with your package manager (brew install node, or nvm install 22). Restart the terminal afterwards.

prerequisites.name: A terminal and a code editor
prerequisites.why: Every step below is a command you type or a file you edit.
prerequisites.get: VS Code (code.visualstudio.com), Cursor or Zed. Open a folder for the project and use the editor's built-in terminal.
prerequisites.verify: You can open a folder and run a command in its terminal

prerequisites.name: Git
prerequisites.why: History for your code, and the way most hosts deploy.
prerequisites.get: Install from git-scm.com or with your package manager, then run git init in the project folder once it exists.

prerequisites.name: A chat webhook URL (Discord, Slack or Telegram)
prerequisites.why: Alerts go to a chat channel you already watch. A webhook URL is the only credential this needs.
prerequisites.get: Discord: Server settings > Integrations > Webhooks > New Webhook, copy the URL. Slack: create an app at api.slack.com/apps, enable Incoming Webhooks, add to a channel, copy the URL. Telegram: create a bot with @BotFather and use the bot token plus your chat id.
prerequisites.verify: curl -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"content":"test"}' <url> posts a message (Discord form; Slack uses a text field)

prerequisites.name: The list of jobs you want watched
prerequisites.why: Each job needs a name, how often it runs, and how late is too late. Deciding this up front is what makes Phase 2 testable.
prerequisites.get: Run crontab -l on each machine and write down every job: name, schedule (every 5 minutes, hourly, nightly at 03:00), and a grace period (how long past due before you want to be told).

prerequisites.name: curl on the machines running the jobs
prerequisites.why: The whole integration is appending && curl -fsS <url> to a crontab line.
prerequisites.get: Already present on nearly every Linux and macOS system.

prerequisites.name: A small always-on server (VPS)
prerequisites.why: This needs one process running all the time with a public address. The monitor must live somewhere other than the machines it watches.
prerequisites.get: Hetzner Cloud (from about 4 EUR), DigitalOcean or Fly.io. Ubuntu 24.04, the smallest size. You need SSH access and a public IP. Only needed for the deploy phase; develop locally first.

prerequisites.name: A domain or subdomain
prerequisites.why: A stable address for ping URLs, so a server move does not mean editing every crontab.
prerequisites.get: Register at Cloudflare Registrar, Porkbun or Namecheap, or use a subdomain of one you already own. You add one DNS record in the deploy phase.
prerequisites.cost: roughly $10 a year, or free on an existing domain

prerequisites.name: Caddy on the server
prerequisites.why: Automatic HTTPS in front of the Node process. Without TLS the browser features this relies on (and your visitors' trust) do not work.
prerequisites.get: On the VPS: follow the install steps at caddyserver.com/docs/install for Ubuntu. One Caddyfile with your domain and a reverse_proxy line is the whole config.
prerequisites.verify: caddy version prints a version on the server

env.name: PORT
env.where: Any free port. Caddy proxies to it on the server.

env.name: DATABASE_PATH
env.where: Where the SQLite file lives. Create the data/ folder; back this file up.

env.name: ALERT_WEBHOOK_URL
env.where: The chat webhook from the prerequisites.

env.name: ALERT_FORMAT
env.where: discord, slack or telegram. Decides the JSON shape of the message.

env.name: ADMIN_USER
env.where: Any username for the basic-auth admin pages.

env.name: ADMIN_PASS
env.where: Generate one: openssl rand -base64 24. Never reuse a real password.

env.name: SITE_URL
env.where: Public base URL, used to print the ping URLs in the dashboard.

env.name: RETENTION_DAYS
env.where: How long to keep individual pings. Alerts and checks are kept forever.

env.name: CHECK_INTERVAL_SECONDS
env.where: How often the loop re-evaluates every check. 30 is plenty.

phases.title: Ping ingestion
phases.goal: Accept pings on URLs that match the Healthchecks scheme, store them, and never fail a ping because the database is busy.

steps.do: Create the project, the database file and the two tables
steps.detail: checks (id uuid, name, period_seconds, grace_seconds, status, last_ping_at, last_started_at, last_duration_ms) and pings (id, check_id, received_at, kind, exit_code, body). All timestamps as UTC epoch milliseconds. Open SQLite with WAL mode and a busy timeout.
commands: mkdir cron-monitor && cd cron-monitor && git init && npm init -y && npm pkg set type=module

steps.do: Route /ping/:uuid and its variants
steps.detail: GET, POST and HEAD on /ping/:uuid is a success. /ping/:uuid/start records a start, /ping/:uuid/fail a failure, /ping/:uuid/log a log line, and /ping/:uuid/<0-255> treats 0 as success and anything else as failure.

steps.do: Store at most 100 kB of a POST body and always answer OK
steps.detail: Read the body up to 100 kB and stop reading. Answer 200 with the plain text OK. An unknown uuid answers 404 with not found and inserts nothing.

steps.do: Add a create-check script for testing
steps.detail: A tiny CLI that inserts a check row with a name, period and grace and prints its ping URL, so you can test before the dashboard exists.

check: curl -fsS http://localhost:3000/ping/<uuid> prints OK and one row appears in pings
Posting a 2 MB body stores exactly 100 kB and still returns 200
A ping to a random uuid returns 404 and creates nothing
/ping/<uuid>/7 stores kind fail with exit_code 7
traps: Store times as UTC epoch milliseconds, never local-time strings. The late maths breaks across a DST change otherwise.
Do not validate the body. Jobs post arbitrary output; you store it and show it.

phases.title: Status state machine
phases.goal: A loop that turns pings into up, late and down, alerts exactly once per transition, and never alerts for a check that has not pinged yet.

steps.do: Write the evaluation function
steps.detail: For each check: up while now is within period of last_ping_at; late once past period; down once past period plus grace. A fail ping sets down at once; any success sets up at once. Status new (never pinged) and paused are skipped.

steps.do: Record every transition in an alerts table
steps.detail: alerts (id, check_id, from_status, to_status, sent_at, delivered, error). Write a row when status changes and only then.

steps.do: Compute run duration from /start to success
steps.detail: When a success follows a start, set last_duration_ms. Show it later so a job that suddenly takes 40 minutes is visible.

steps.do: Run the loop on CHECK_INTERVAL_SECONDS in the same process
steps.detail: setInterval, wrapped in try/catch so one bad row cannot stop the loop. Log one line per transition.

check: A check with period 60 and grace 30 reads up right after a ping, late at 61 seconds and down at 91
Exactly one alerts row per transition and none for a repeated loop in the same state
A fail ping flips a check to down immediately
A new check with no pings never gets an alerts row
traps: Test the state machine with a fake clock before touching the webhook. Waiting real minutes to see a transition is how this phase eats an evening.

phases.title: Alerting
phases.goal: One chat message when a job goes down, one when it recovers, retries that never stall the loop.

steps.do: Write a sender for your ALERT_FORMAT
steps.detail: Discord wants {content}, Slack wants {text}, Telegram wants chat_id and text on the bot API. Include the check name, the new status, how late in human units (14 min late) and the last failure body if any.

steps.do: Drain undelivered alerts rows after each loop
steps.detail: Send, mark delivered on 2xx. On failure retry three times with backoff (2 s, 10 s, 60 s), then record the error on the row and move on.

steps.do: Send a recovery message on the return to up
steps.detail: It carries how long the outage lasted, from the down alert's sent_at.

check: Taking a check down produces exactly one message in the channel
Leaving it down produces no further messages
Recovery produces exactly one message with a duration
Pointing ALERT_WEBHOOK_URL at a URL that returns 500 leaves an alerts row with an error and the loop still running

phases.title: Admin dashboard
phases.goal: Create and manage checks in the browser, and see every job's state at a glance.

steps.do: Add basic auth from ADMIN_USER and ADMIN_PASS
steps.detail: Compare with a constant-time function. Everything under /admin requires it; /ping never does.

steps.do: Build the check list
steps.detail: One row per check: a green, amber or red dot, name, relative last ping (7 min ago), period and grace, and the ping URL with a copy button plus a ready-to-paste crontab example line.

steps.do: Add create, edit, pause and delete forms
steps.detail: Plain HTML forms posting to /admin routes. No JavaScript required for any of them.

steps.do: Draw a 24-hour ping histogram per check as inline SVG
steps.detail: One bar per hour from a GROUP BY on received_at. No chart library.

check: A check can be created, edited, paused and deleted from the browser
The page renders correctly with zero checks
The histogram bars match a count query for the last 24 hours
The ping URL copied from the dashboard works in curl

phases.title: Hardening and deploy
phases.goal: Live on your VPS behind HTTPS, surviving restarts, with old pings pruned.

steps.do: Rate limit /ping per IP, generously
steps.detail: A legitimate job may ping every minute; allow 120 per minute per IP in memory and answer 429 beyond that.

steps.do: Add /healthz and a nightly retention job
steps.detail: /healthz answers 200 with a quick database read. Retention deletes pings older than RETENTION_DAYS once a day; alerts and checks are never pruned.

steps.do: Install on the VPS with systemd and Caddy
steps.detail: Unit with Restart=on-failure, EnvironmentFile=.env, an unprivileged user. Caddyfile: your domain with reverse_proxy localhost:PORT.
commands: sudo cp deploy/monitor.service /etc/systemd/system/ && sudo systemctl enable --now monitor

steps.do: Add the ping to one real crontab and write the README
steps.detail: README: the one-liner (*/5 * * * * /path/job.sh && curl -fsS <url>), the wrapper form that reports failures with /start and /fail, and the same-host warning.

check: The service comes back with state intact after sudo reboot
Retention actually deletes pings older than the window
A real cron job on another machine shows up as up on the dashboard
The README takes a reader from clone to a monitored job
traps: Put the monitor on a different machine than the jobs. On the same host it dies with the host, which is precisely when it was supposed to speak.

phases.title: Operate it like a product
phases.goal: Only for the product-builder path: know when the monitor itself is down, never lose the database, and keep the server patched.

steps.do: Add a /healthz endpoint and an external uptime check against it
steps.detail: Answer 200 with the build id and a quick database read. Point a free uptime monitor (or your own, from the Healthchecks entry on this site) at it so an outage is noticed before a user notices.

steps.do: Write structured request logs and rotate them
steps.detail: One JSON line per request: method, path, status, duration, no raw IPs. Rotate weekly with logrotate, keep eight.

steps.do: Back the SQLite file up off the machine nightly and test a restore
steps.detail: SQLite's .backup command makes a consistent copy while the app runs. Copy it to object storage or a second machine; then, once, restore it into a fresh checkout and confirm the app reads it.

steps.do: Lock the box down
steps.detail: Firewall allowing only 22, 80 and 443; unattended security updates on; the app running as an unprivileged user under systemd with Restart=on-failure.

check: Stopping the service triggers an uptime alert within a few minutes
A restore from last night's backup contains yesterday's data
A port scan from another machine shows only 22, 80 and 443

product.outcome: A monitoring service others could rely on: every job watched from a box that is not theirs, alerts that fire once and recover, and the monitor itself monitored and backed up.

architecture.owns: the /ping routes and the pings table
architecture.swap: Any HTTP listener writing the same rows; the scheme is Healthchecks-compatible so clients never change

architecture.owns: the state machine and the alerts table
architecture.swap: Pure function over rows; testable with a fake clock, replaceable without touching ingest

architecture.owns: formatting and delivering alerts with retries
architecture.swap: One function per ALERT_FORMAT; add email or SMS as another adapter
Any UI over the same tables; the ping URLs are the contract

operations.backup: SQLite .backup nightly to object storage, thirty days kept. The checks table is the valuable part; pings are replaceable.
operations.restore: Copy the backup to DATABASE_PATH, start the service, confirm the dashboard lists every check and pings resume.
operations.monitoring: An external uptime check on /healthz from a different provider than the VPS. Watch the alerts table for rows with an error: that is the webhook breaking.
operations.incident: If the monitor is down, jobs are unwatched but unaffected; restore and re-check the last few hours by hand. If the webhook leaks, rotate it in the chat tool and update .env.

releaseGate: A clean clone reaches a monitored job using only the README
Every transition alerts exactly once in a soak test of one flapping and one stable check
One restore drill performed and dated in OPERATIONS.md
The monitor runs on a different provider than the jobs it watches

notIncluded: SMS, WhatsApp and phone-call alerts. One webhook into a chat app covers the solo case; a provider bill covers the rest.
Status pages, teams and on-call rotation. That is the paid product.
Cron-expression parsing and insights. Period plus grace is enough and it is the part you can get right.
after: A second alert channel (email over SMTP) behind the same Notifier interface
A public read-only status page rendered from the checks table
